latam: Caplin sells mostly in small Central American and Caribbean markets (Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Panama, Costa Rica), where multinationals sell brands and local makers are small; >80% of its LatAm revenue is private market (pharmacies), the rest government tenders (ICICI Direct Q3FY26 call notes; Ashok Partheeban: 18-20% institutional in Central America).

Registrations are the entry barrier: 951 products registered in Guatemala, 689 in Nicaragua, 632 in Honduras, 504 in the Dominican Republic, 468 in El Salvador, 354 in Ecuador (AR FY26 registration map). Each new market (Chile, Mexico, Colombia) takes years of filings and bio-studies.
Larger markets are tender-heavy (Mexico, Chile); Mexico gives local manufacturers a price advantage in public tenders (management: 16%; ICICI Direct: 10-15% on margin).

Currencies: El Salvador, Panama and Ecuador use the US dollar; Guatemala and Costa Rica are stable; Nicaragua and Honduras move 3-4% (Chairman, 14-May-2026). The rupee fell from an average ₹88.4/$ in FY26 to ₹94.65/$ at Mar-26 (AR FY26 AOC-1), which lifts rupee revenue.
us: US sterile injectables: chronic shortages of older injectables keep pricing better than in oral generics; three large wholesalers control ~70% of distribution (Chairman: Caplin targets the remaining ~30% through IDNs and hospital systems).
Capacity and compliance are the constraints: sterile lines take 2-3 years to build and qualify; a USFDA warning letter or import alert can stop supplies from a single-site company.
Generic tariffs: the US administration announced a waiver of tariffs on generics with effect two years out (question on the 12-Aug-2026 call); Caplin manufactures in India.

moat: Distribution and registrations in small LatAm markets

5,000+ registrations; own subsidiaries, warehouses and 700+ people; 41% shelf share in independent pharmacies (Ashok Partheeban); 20 years of presence. Hard for an Indian rival to copy quickly; but the markets are small and slow (Central America +7% in FY26).
Stock-and-sale model (inventory next to the customer)
Six months of stock in the market protects supply and lets Caplin price up when inputs rise; the cost is 181 inventory days and 136 receivable days.
40% outsourced from Indian and Chinese makers keeps capital light; gross margin ~60%; not unique.
60 ANDAs, own label, 30+ IDN contracts; but one site, capacity-constrained, now carrying a 10-observation 483; peers (Gland, Aurobindo, Zydus, Eugia) are far larger.
Mostly plain generics; branded generics only ~5% of sales by value in 2012 rising to 25% (company chart); brand marketing in CNS started only in Sep-2026 in three markets.
moatVerdict: A real but narrow moat: a distribution and registration franchise in small Latin American markets that throws off cash, but whose growth in dollars has slowed to low single digits; the US business is promising and fast-growing but has no moat yet and a fresh compliance flag.
critiques: Growth in dollars is slow: LatAm sales rose only from $150 mn to $155 mn in FY26; much of the rupee growth is the falling rupee and lumpy tenders (El Salvador).
Working capital is heavy and rising: receivables 138 days (Screener), inventory 181 days; Q1FY27 operating cash flow fell to ₹95 cr.

The CCPS held by Eight Roads / F-Prime convert into at least 25.29% of Caplin Steriles, yet the accounts attribute none of its profit to them: Caplin Point's reported EPS overstates its economic share of the US business.
Single US site: the 13-21 Aug 2026 inspection ended with 10 observations; the US is 22% of revenue and most of the growth story.
Founder-led and family-run: two sons are non-executive vice-chairmen; the Chairman's calls are long on philosophy and short on numbers; no formal guidance.
Cash pile (₹1,480 cr, ~8% of market value) earns ~6.4%; management talks of acquisitions (distributors, ANDAs) and is moving into credit funds.
gaps: Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Africa revenue by country is not disclosed (only LatAm $155 mn, Africa ~3%, Central America +7%).
